subject: ENGGW
title: English – Grammar and Writing
status: DRAFT — for review by an English teacher before any question is approved
source: Written to the CBSE English Language and Literature (184) syllabus for 2025-26, Section B for Class X: grammar assessed through gap filling, editing and transformation, and the formal letter and analytical paragraph writing tasks. No book text is quoted.

questions.stem: Riya wants to become ______ engineer when she finishes school.
questions.explanation: 'An' is used before a word that begins with a vowel sound, and 'engineer' begins with a vowel sound.

questions.stem: Our school has invited ______ European scientist to speak at the science exhibition next week.
questions.explanation: The choice between 'a' and 'an' depends on sound, not spelling. 'European' begins with a 'yoo' (consonant) sound, so it takes 'a'.

questions.stem: Arjun took ______ hour-long test on Monday and then spent the evening at the badminton court.
questions.explanation: The 'h' in 'hour' is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound and takes 'an'.

questions.stem: There is very ______ milk left in the fridge, so please buy a packet on your way home from tuition.
questions.explanation: 'Milk' is uncountable, so it takes 'little', not 'few' or 'many'. 'Very little' means hardly any, which is why more must be bought.

questions.stem: The new library has so ______ books on astronomy that the senior students cannot decide where to begin.
questions.explanation: 'Books' is a plural countable noun, so it takes 'many'. 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns, and 'a lot' and 'lots' need 'of' and cannot follow 'so'.

questions.stem: Although the team practised hard, it had ______ chance of winning against the defending champions, and most spectators expected it to lose.
questions.explanation: 'Chance' used in this sense is uncountable, so it takes 'little', which means almost none. 'Few', 'many' and 'several' go with plural countable nouns.

questions.stem: ______ mangoes in this basket are riper than the ones on that shelf.
questions.explanation: A plural noun near the speaker takes the demonstrative 'these'; 'this' and 'that' go with singular nouns.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
My uncle is a honest shopkeeper who never overcharges his customers.
questions.explanation: The 'h' in 'honest' is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound and needs 'an'.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
The principal gave us an useful piece of advice before the board examinations began.
questions.explanation: 'Useful' begins with a 'yoo' (consonant) sound, so it takes 'a', even though it is spelt with a vowel.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
We did not have many time to visit the museum because the bus left early.
questions.explanation: 'Time' in the sense of duration is uncountable, so in a negative sentence it takes 'much', not 'many' or 'few'.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
Every students in the class has submitted the project on rainwater harvesting.
questions.explanation: 'Every' is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb: 'Every student has submitted'.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system. A Earth takes about 365 days to go round it.
questions.explanation: The Earth is unique, so it takes the definite article 'the'. 'A' can never come before a vowel sound in any case.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
Only a little students turned up for the extra class because of the heavy rain.
questions.explanation: 'Students' is a plural countable noun, so it takes 'a few'. 'A little' and 'much' are used with uncountable nouns.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
Kabir has been learning to play the guitar for a year and wants to join an university band next year.
questions.explanation: 'University' begins with a 'yoo' (consonant) sound, so it takes 'a'.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence using 'a few' without changing its meaning: 'Some students, though not many, stayed back to decorate the hall.'

options.text: A few of students stayed back to decorate the hall.
Few students stayed back to decorate the hall.
A few students stayed back to decorate the hall.
A little students stayed back to decorate the hall.

questions.explanation: 'A few' comes directly before a plural countable noun and means 'some, a small number'. 'Few' without 'a' means 'hardly any', which changes the meaning.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence using 'not much': 'There is only a small amount of sugar in the jar.'

options.text: There are not much sugar in the jar.
There is not much sugar in the jar.
There is not many sugar in the jar.
There is not much sugars in the jar.

questions.explanation: 'Sugar' is uncountable: it takes 'much', stays singular and takes the singular verb 'is'.

questions.stem: Combine the two sentences into one, using the articles correctly: 'I saw a dog. The dog was chasing a cat.'

options.text: I saw an dog which was chasing a cat.
I saw dog which was chasing a cat.
I saw a dog which was chasing cat.
I saw a dog which was chasing a cat.

questions.explanation: A singular countable noun mentioned for the first time needs 'a' or 'an', and 'dog' and 'cat' begin with consonant sounds, so both take 'a'.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence so that it begins with 'Many': 'A large number of volunteers joined the tree-planting drive in Chennai.'

options.text: Many volunteers joined the tree-planting drive in Chennai.
Many volunteer joined the tree-planting drive in Chennai.
Many of volunteers joined the tree-planting drive in Chennai.
Many a volunteers joined the tree-planting drive in Chennai.

questions.explanation: 'Many' is followed directly by a plural noun. 'Many of' needs a determiner such as 'the' after it, and 'many a' takes a singular noun.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence using a possessive determiner: 'The bicycle that belongs to Meera and her brother has a flat tyre.'

options.text: There bicycle has a flat tyre.
Theirs bicycle has a flat tyre.
Their bicycle has a flat tyre.
Her bicycle has a flat tyre.

questions.explanation: The bicycle belongs to two people, so the possessive determiner is 'their'. 'Theirs' is a pronoun that stands alone, and 'there' is an adverb of place.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence using 'Each': 'All the participants received a certificate.'

options.text: Each of participant received a certificate.
Each the participants received a certificate.

questions.explanation: 'Each' is followed by a singular noun; 'each of' would need 'the' and a plural noun.

questions.stem: Look! The children ______ a sandcastle near the waves.
questions.explanation: 'Look!' shows the action is happening now, so the present continuous is needed.

questions.stem: By the time the ambulance arrived, the neighbours ______ the injured cyclist to the side of the road.
questions.explanation: An action completed before another past action ('arrived') is in the past perfect.

questions.stem: Priya is exhausted because she ______ for the district chess championship since six o'clock this morning.
questions.explanation: An action that began in the past and is still going on, with 'since', takes the present perfect continuous. The past perfect continuous does not fit a present situation ('is exhausted').

questions.stem: If it ______ tomorrow, the inter-house football match will be postponed.
questions.explanation: In a first conditional, the 'if' clause takes the simple present and the main clause takes 'will'.

questions.stem: The water crisis in our town is not new. For the past five years, the level of groundwater ______ steadily, and experts warn that it will fall further.
questions.explanation: 'For the past five years' describes a continuing process up to now, which needs the present perfect continuous.

questions.stem: Rohan ______ his homework when the power went off last night.
questions.explanation: An action in progress in the past when another action interrupted it takes the past continuous.

questions.stem: By December next year, the new metro line from the airport to the city centre ______.
questions.explanation: 'By' a future time takes the future perfect, and since the line does not complete itself, the passive 'will have been completed' is required.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
Yesterday our class goes on a trip to the planetarium.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' marks a finished past time, so the simple past 'went' is needed. The present perfect cannot be used with a finished past time.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
I have visited Jaipur with my family in 2023.
questions.explanation: A definite past time such as 'in 2023' takes the simple past, not the present perfect.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
During the quiz yesterday, she was knowing the answer to every question.
questions.explanation: 'Know' is a stative verb and is not normally used in continuous forms; with 'yesterday' the simple past 'knew' is correct.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
The team had been training for three months before the tournament, and they win the trophy easily.

options.text: had been training → has been training

questions.explanation: The whole account is in the past, so the second action also takes the simple past: 'won'.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
Hardly had the bell rang when the students rushed out of the classroom.
questions.explanation: The past perfect is 'had' plus the past participle, and the past participle of 'ring' is 'rung'.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
Scientists have been study the melting of Himalayan glaciers for over two decades.
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous is 'have/has been' plus the -ing form of the verb.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
When I reached the station, the train already left, so I took an auto-rickshaw home.
questions.explanation: The train left before I reached, so the earlier past action takes the past perfect.

questions.stem: Rewrite in the present perfect continuous tense: 'Ananya started learning Kathak four years ago, and she is still learning it.'

options.text: Ananya has been learning Kathak since four years.
Ananya is learning Kathak since four years.
Ananya has been learning Kathak for four years.
Ananya had been learning Kathak for four years.

questions.explanation: An action continuing up to now takes 'has been' plus -ing. 'For' goes with a length of time; 'since' goes with a point in time.

questions.stem: Change the sentence into the past continuous tense: 'The farmers harvest the wheat in the fields.'

options.text: The farmers were harvesting the wheat in the fields.
The farmers was harvesting the wheat in the fields.
The farmers had harvested the wheat in the fields.
The farmers are harvesting the wheat in the fields.

questions.explanation: The past continuous is 'was/were' plus -ing, and the plural subject 'farmers' takes 'were'.

questions.stem: Combine into one sentence using 'before', putting the earlier action in the past perfect: 'We finished decorating the hall. Then the guests arrived.'

options.text: We had finished decorating the hall before the guests will arrive.
We have finished decorating the hall before the guests arrived.
The guests had arrived before we finished decorating the hall.
We had finished decorating the hall before the guests arrived.

questions.explanation: The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect and the later one the simple past. Swapping them reverses what happened.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence using 'will': 'Our school is going to open the new computer lab next week.'

options.text: Our school will opens the new computer lab next week.
Our school will open the new computer lab next week.
Our school will opened the new computer lab next week.
Our school would open the new computer lab next week.

questions.explanation: 'Will' is always followed by the base form of the verb.

questions.stem: Rewrite in the passive voice, keeping the same tense: 'The municipal workers are repairing the potholes on our street.'

options.text: The potholes on our street are being repaired by the municipal workers.
The potholes on our street are repaired by the municipal workers.
The potholes on our street have been repaired by the municipal workers.
The potholes on our street were being repaired by the municipal workers.

questions.explanation: The present continuous passive is 'am/is/are being' plus the past participle.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence, replacing 'every July' with 'last July' and changing the verb as needed: 'The heavy rain floods the low-lying areas of the city every July.'

options.text: The heavy rain floods the low-lying areas of the city last July.
The heavy rain has flooded the low-lying areas of the city last July.
The heavy rain flooded the low-lying areas of the city last July.
The heavy rain had flooded the low-lying areas of the city last July.

questions.explanation: 'Last July' is a finished past time, so the simple past is used; the present perfect cannot take a finished time expression.

questions.stem: You ______ wear a helmet while riding a two-wheeler; it is the law.
questions.explanation: 'Must' expresses a strong obligation, such as a rule or a law.

questions.stem: ______ I borrow your notes on chemical reactions, please? I missed yesterday's class.
questions.explanation: 'May I…?' is a polite way to ask for permission. 'Ought' needs 'to', and 'must' and 'would' do not ask permission.

questions.stem: When he was only six, my brother ______ swim across the river.
questions.explanation: Ability in the past is expressed with 'could'.

questions.stem: The roads are wet and the sky is dark; it ______ rained heavily during the night.
questions.explanation: A confident conclusion about the past, drawn from evidence, uses 'must have' plus the past participle.

questions.stem: You look very tired, Karan. You ______ take a short break before you start the next chapter.
questions.explanation: Advice is given with 'should'. 'Ought' and 'need' would both require 'to' here.

questions.stem: Students ______ not bring mobile phones into the examination hall; anyone found with one will be disqualified.
questions.explanation: 'Must not' expresses prohibition. 'Need not' means something is not necessary, which contradicts the penalty in the sentence.

questions.stem: If you had left home ten minutes earlier, you ______ caught the school bus.
questions.explanation: In a third conditional, 'if' plus the past perfect is followed by 'would have' plus the past participle.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
She can speaks three languages fluently.
questions.explanation: A modal is always followed by the base form of the verb, without -s.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
You ought obey the traffic rules even when there is no policeman around.
questions.explanation: 'Ought' is always followed by 'to' and the base form of the verb.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
We must to finish the science project before Friday.
questions.explanation: 'Must' is followed directly by the base form, never by 'to'.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
He should have informed the teacher yesterday, but he could not came to school.
questions.explanation: After a modal such as 'could not', the verb is in its base form: 'come'.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
The match is not tomorrow, so you need not to come to the stadium early.
questions.explanation: Used as a modal, 'need not' is followed by the base form without 'to'.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
May you please pass me the salt?
questions.explanation: 'May' asks permission for the speaker ('May I…?'). A polite request for someone else to act uses 'Could you…?' or 'Would you…?'.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
When I was younger, I would to play cricket in the lane every evening.
questions.explanation: 'Would' for a past habit is followed by the base form without 'to'.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence using a modal of permission: 'The students are allowed to use the library after school hours.'

options.text: The students must use the library after school hours.
The students may to use the library after school hours.
The students may use the library after school hours.
The students may uses the library after school hours.

questions.explanation: 'May' expresses permission and takes the base form. 'Must' would turn permission into an obligation.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence using a modal of obligation: 'It is necessary for all visitors to show their identity cards at the gate.'

options.text: All visitors must showing their identity cards at the gate.
All visitors must show their identity cards at the gate.
All visitors may show their identity cards at the gate.
All visitors must shows their identity cards at the gate.

questions.explanation: Obligation is expressed with 'must' plus the base form. 'May' would only give permission.

questions.stem: Rewrite the command as a polite request using a modal: 'Open the window.'

options.text: Could you please opened the window?
Must you please open the window?
Could you please to open the window?
Could you please open the window?

questions.explanation: A polite request uses 'Could you…?' followed by the base form of the verb.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence using 'must have': 'I am sure that Aditi forgot her lunch box at home.'

options.text: Aditi must have forgot her lunch box at home.
Aditi must had forgotten her lunch box at home.
Aditi must forgotten her lunch box at home.
Aditi must have forgotten her lunch box at home.

questions.explanation: A certain deduction about the past is 'must have' plus the past participle; the past participle of 'forget' is 'forgotten'.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence using 'should' to give advice: 'It is a good idea for you to drink more water in summer.'

options.text: You should to drink more water in summer.
You should drink more water in summer.
You should drinks more water in summer.
You must not drink more water in summer.

questions.explanation: Advice is given with 'should' followed by the base form of the verb.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence using 'can': 'Rahul is able to solve this puzzle in two minutes.'

options.text: Rahul can solves this puzzle in two minutes.
Rahul can able to solve this puzzle in two minutes.
Rahul can solve this puzzle in two minutes.
Rahul cans solve this puzzle in two minutes.

questions.explanation: 'Can' expresses ability, never takes -s, and is followed by the base form.

questions.stem: Each of the players ______ given a new jersey before the final.
questions.explanation: 'Each of' plus a plural noun is still singular, so it takes a singular verb.

questions.stem: Neither the captain nor the other players ______ happy with the umpire's decision.
questions.explanation: With 'neither…nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject; 'players' is plural, and the context is past.

questions.stem: The teacher, along with her students, ______ planting saplings in the school garden.
questions.explanation: A phrase introduced by 'along with' does not change the subject; the subject is 'the teacher', which is singular.

questions.stem: Mathematics ______ my favourite subject, although physics is catching up fast.
questions.explanation: Names of subjects ending in -s, such as mathematics and physics, are singular.

questions.stem: Bread and butter ______ what my grandfather eats for breakfast every day.
questions.explanation: Two nouns joined by 'and' that together name a single dish or idea take a singular verb.

questions.stem: Twenty kilometres ______ a long distance to walk in the afternoon heat.
questions.explanation: A plural amount of distance, money or time thought of as one quantity takes a singular verb.

questions.stem: Either the students or their class teacher ______ going to present the report at the assembly.
questions.explanation: With 'either…or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'their class teacher', which is singular.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
My brother and I goes to school by the same bus every morning.
questions.explanation: Two subjects joined by 'and' make a plural subject, which takes 'go'.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
One of the boys in our class have won a scholarship to study robotics.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'one', which is singular; 'of the boys' does not change it.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
The news about the floods in Assam are very disturbing.
questions.explanation: 'News' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb, whatever follows it.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
Every student and every teacher were present at the Independence Day celebrations.
questions.explanation: When each subject joined by 'and' is preceded by 'every' or 'each', the verb is singular.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
The number of students using public transport has risen this year. A number of them says the new bus route saves time.
questions.explanation: 'The number of' is singular, but 'a number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
Neither of the two answers are correct, so the teacher asked us to try again.
questions.explanation: 'Neither of' plus a plural noun takes a singular verb in standard usage.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
The quality of the mangoes sold in these markets have improved over the years.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'the quality', which is singular; the phrase 'of the mangoes sold in these markets' between them does not change the verb.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence beginning with 'Each': 'All the rooms in the hostel have a study table.'

options.text: Each room in the hostel have a study table.
Each rooms in the hostel has a study table.
Each room in the hostel has a study table.
Each of room in the hostel has a study table.

questions.explanation: 'Each' takes a singular noun and a singular verb.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence beginning with 'The coach, as well as the players,': 'The coach and the players are travelling to Kolkata.'

options.text: The coach, as well as the players, is travelling to Kolkata.
The coach, as well as the players, are travelling to Kolkata.
The coach, as well as the players, were travelling to Kolkata.
The coach, as well as the players, have travelling to Kolkata.

questions.explanation: A phrase with 'as well as' is not part of the subject; the verb agrees with 'the coach', which is singular.

questions.stem: Combine the sentences using 'neither…nor': 'My sister does not like spinach. My parents do not like spinach either.'

options.text: Neither my sister nor my parents likes spinach.
Neither my sister nor my parents like spinach.
Neither my sister or my parents like spinach.
Neither my sister nor my parents doesn't like spinach.

questions.explanation: 'Neither' pairs with 'nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject ('parents', plural), and no second negative is added.

questions.stem: Change the subject to the plural and make the verb agree: 'The child plays in the park every evening.'

options.text: The children play in the park every evening.
The children plays in the park every evening.
The childrens play in the park every evening.
The child play in the park every evening.

questions.explanation: The plural of 'child' is 'children', and a plural subject takes the verb without -s.

questions.stem: Combine the sentences using 'either…or': 'Ravi cleans the laboratory on Saturdays, or his friends clean it.'

options.text: Either Ravi or his friends cleans the laboratory on Saturdays.
Either Ravi nor his friends clean the laboratory on Saturdays.
Either Ravi or his friends cleaning the laboratory on Saturdays.
Either Ravi or his friends clean the laboratory on Saturdays.

questions.explanation: 'Either' pairs with 'or', and the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'his friends', which is plural.

questions.stem: Rewrite the sentence beginning with 'Neither of the two bridges': 'Both the bridges over the river are unsafe for heavy vehicles.'

options.text: Neither of the two bridges are safe for heavy vehicles.
Neither of the two bridges is not safe for heavy vehicles.
Neither of the two bridges is safe for heavy vehicles.
Neither of the two bridges have safe for heavy vehicles.

questions.explanation: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb, and since 'neither' is already negative, no 'not' is added.

questions.stem:
Direct: Neha said, "I am tired after the long rehearsal."
Reported: Neha said that she ______ tired after the long rehearsal.
questions.explanation: When the reporting verb is in the past, the present tense changes to the past: 'am' becomes 'was'.

questions.stem: The librarian asked me ______ I had returned the atlas.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question is reported with 'if' or 'whether', never with 'that'.

questions.stem: The doctor ______ my grandfather to walk for thirty minutes every day.
questions.explanation: Advice is reported with 'advised' plus the person plus 'to' and the verb. 'Said' and 'suggested' cannot take a person followed by 'to'.

questions.stem:
Direct: The coach said to Aman, "Where did you keep the cricket kit?"
Reported: The coach asked Aman where ______ the cricket kit.
questions.explanation: A reported question uses statement word order (subject before verb), and the simple past changes to the past perfect.

questions.stem:
Direct: Ishaan said, "I will call you tomorrow."
Reported: Ishaan said that he ______ call me the next day.
questions.explanation: After a past reporting verb, 'will' changes to 'would', and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.

questions.stem: The teacher told the students ______ make noise in the corridor.
questions.explanation: A negative command is reported with 'not to' plus the base form of the verb.

questions.stem:
Aarav asked his sister, "Have you finished the science project?" When she said she had not, he asked, "When are you planning to finish it?"
Reported: Aarav asked his sister when she ______ to finish the project.
questions.explanation: In a reported question the present continuous moves back to the past continuous, and the subject comes before the verb.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
Mira said that she is going to Shimla the following week.
questions.explanation: When the reporting verb is past, the present continuous changes to the past continuous: 'was going'.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
The visitor asked the guard where was the principal's office.

options.text: was the principal's office → the principal's office was

questions.explanation: A reported question takes statement word order: subject first, then verb.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
The officer ordered the soldiers to stood in a line.
questions.explanation: A reported command is 'ordered' plus the person plus 'to' and the base form of the verb.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
My mother asked me that whether I had eaten my lunch.
questions.explanation: A reported yes/no question is introduced by 'whether' or 'if' alone; 'that' is used only for statements.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
Kavya said that she had visited the science museum yesterday and that she had enjoyed the robotics section.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, words of time shift with the tense: 'yesterday' becomes 'the previous day' or 'the day before'.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
The old man requested the boy help him cross the busy road.
questions.explanation: A reported request is 'requested' plus the person plus 'to' and the base form of the verb.

questions.stem:
The sentence below contains one error. Choose the option that corrects it.
Rahul asked his friend if he will come to the match the following day.
questions.explanation: After a past reporting verb, 'will' changes to 'would' in the reported question.

questions.stem: Change into reported speech: The principal said, "The school will remain closed tomorrow because of the cyclone warning."

options.text: The principal said that the school will remain closed tomorrow because of the cyclone warning.
The principal told that the school would remain closed the next day because of the cyclone warning.
The principal said that the school would remain closed the next day because of the cyclone warning.
The principal said that the school will remain closed the next day because of the cyclone warning.

questions.explanation: 'Will' becomes 'would' and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'. 'Told' needs a listener after it, so 'told that' is wrong.

questions.stem: Change into reported speech: Sanjay said to me, "I have lost my library card here."

options.text: Sanjay told me that I had lost my library card there.
Sanjay told me that he had lost his library card there.
Sanjay said me that he had lost his library card there.
Sanjay told me that he has lost his library card here.

questions.explanation: 'Said to me' becomes 'told me'; 'I' and 'my' become 'he' and 'his'; the present perfect becomes the past perfect; and 'here' becomes 'there'.

questions.stem: Change into reported speech: The shopkeeper said to Mr Iyer, "Do you want a paper bag?"

options.text: The shopkeeper asked Mr Iyer if did he want a paper bag.
The shopkeeper asked Mr Iyer that he wanted a paper bag.
The shopkeeper said to Mr Iyer if he wants a paper bag.
The shopkeeper asked Mr Iyer if he wanted a paper bag.

questions.explanation: A yes/no question is reported with 'asked' plus 'if' or 'whether', statement word order and no 'do/did', and the simple present moves to the simple past.

questions.stem: Change into reported speech: The teacher said to Divya, "Why are you late today?"

options.text: The teacher asked Divya why she was late that day.
The teacher asked Divya why was she late that day.
The teacher asked Divya why she is late today.
The teacher asked Divya that why she was late that day.

questions.explanation: A wh-question keeps its question word but takes statement word order; 'are' becomes 'was' and 'today' becomes 'that day'.

questions.stem: Change into reported speech: The coach said to the players, "Warm up properly before the match."

options.text: The coach told the players that warm up properly before the match.
The coach said the players to warm up properly before the match.
The coach told the players to warm up properly before the match.
The coach told to the players warm up properly before the match.

questions.explanation: A command is reported with a verb such as 'told' or 'ordered', the listener, and 'to' plus the base form of the verb.

questions.stem: Change into reported speech: Ritika said to her brother, "Please don't touch my paintings."

options.text: Ritika requested her brother to not touch my paintings.
Ritika requested to her brother not to touch her paintings.
Ritika requested her brother not to touch her paintings.
Ritika said her brother please don't touch her paintings.

questions.explanation: 'Please' signals a request, reported with 'requested' plus the listener plus 'not to'; 'please' is dropped and 'my' becomes 'her'.

A request to publish the letter to draw the authorities' attention
The problem described: loudspeakers after 10 p.m. during the examination season

Suggestions: enforcing the time limit on loudspeakers, police action on complaints, residents keeping volume low, awareness
A concluding appeal

questions.stem: A bar chart shows the average daily screen time, in hours, of 200 Class 10 students in a school, divided by activity, on weekdays and at weekends. Weekdays: study and online classes 1.5 hours, social media 1.0 hour, gaming 0.5 hours, watching videos 1.0 hour (total 4.0 hours). Weekends: study and online classes 1.0 hour, social media 2.0 hours, gaming 1.5 hours, watching videos 2.5 hours (total 7.0 hours). Write an analytical paragraph of 100-120 words describing and comparing the data and drawing a conclusion.
valuePoints: Introduction: what the bar chart shows (daily screen time of 200 Class 10 students by activity, weekdays against weekends)
Total screen time rises from 4 hours on weekdays to 7 hours at weekends, an increase of 3 hours (75%)
Study is the largest use on weekdays (1.5 hours) but falls to 1 hour at weekends, the only activity that decreases
Entertainment rises sharply at weekends: videos 1 to 2.5 hours, social media doubles to 2 hours, gaming triples to 1.5 hours
Supported conclusion: leisure, not study, drives weekend screen time, so students may need to balance weekend screen use

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Accurate figures, the main trend and the key comparisons, with a conclusion the data supports

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Introduction, analysis and conclusion in a coherent single paragraph with linking words

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Correct grammar, spelling and vocabulary of comparison and change

questions.stem: A line graph shows the average daily water use per person, in litres, in the town of Rampur from 2019 to 2025: 2019 - 150, 2020 - 165, 2021 - 172, 2022 - 160, 2023 - 140, 2024 - 128, 2025 - 120. A note under the graph says that water meters were installed in every home and rainwater harvesting was made compulsory for new buildings at the start of 2022. Write an analytical paragraph of 100-120 words describing the trend and drawing a conclusion.
valuePoints: Introduction: what the graph shows (daily water use per person in Rampur, 2019-2025)
Rise from 150 litres in 2019 to a peak of 172 litres in 2021
Steady fall every year from 2022, reaching 120 litres in 2025, 52 litres below the peak and 30 litres (20%) below 2019
The turning point coincides with the meters and rainwater harvesting introduced in 2022
Supported conclusion: the measures appear to have encouraged saving water, though the graph alone cannot prove they were the only cause

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Rise, peak, turning point and fall described with correct figures, linked to the 2022 measures

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Chronological, well-linked paragraph with an introduction and a conclusion

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Correct grammar and precise vocabulary of trends (peaked, declined steadily)

95% of students (760) take part in some sport; only 5% (40) take none

questions.stem: A table shows the share of electricity generated from each source in a state in 2015 and 2025. Coal: 70% in 2015, 52% in 2025. Hydro: 12%, 13%. Solar: 3%, 18%. Wind: 5%, 10%. Natural gas: 7%, 4%. Nuclear: 3%, 3%. Write an analytical paragraph of 100-120 words describing the changes, comparing the sources and drawing a conclusion.
valuePoints: Introduction: what the table shows (share of electricity by source in a state, 2015 and 2025)
Coal remains the largest source but its share falls by 18 percentage points, from 70% to 52%
Solar grows six-fold, from 3% to 18%, and wind doubles from 5% to 10%, becoming the second and fourth largest sources
Hydro rises slightly (12% to 13%), natural gas falls (7% to 4%), nuclear is unchanged at 3%
Renewables (hydro, solar, wind) rise from 20% to 41% of the total
Supported conclusion: the state is shifting towards clean energy, though coal still supplies about half its electricity

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Major changes quantified correctly, sources compared, and a balanced conclusion

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Grouped logically (falling, rising, stable) with an introduction and conclusion

rubric.label: Accuracy

questions.stem: A double bar chart shows the results of a survey of the same 400 students of a school in 2021 and 2025, asking how they prefer to read for pleasure. 2021: printed books 60% (240 students), e-books 25% (100), audiobooks 5% (20), do not read for pleasure 10% (40). 2025: printed books 45% (180), e-books 30% (120), audiobooks 15% (60), do not read for pleasure 10% (40). Write an analytical paragraph of 100-120 words describing and comparing the data and drawing a conclusion.
valuePoints: Introduction: what the chart shows (reading preferences of 400 students, 2021 and 2025)
Printed books remain the most preferred but fall from 60% to 45% (240 to 180 students)
Digital formats grow: e-books from 25% to 30%, audiobooks triple from 5% to 15%; together from 30% to 45%, equal to print in 2025
The share who do not read for pleasure stays at 10% (40 students)
Supported conclusion: students are not reading less but are moving from print to digital formats, so libraries could add e-books and audiobooks

rubric.label: Content

rubric.label: Organisation

questions.stem: Two maps show the town of Navpur in 2001 and 2021. In 2001 Navpur covered 40 square kilometres and had a population of 7.5 lakh. It had farmland to its north, one bridge across the river, a lake of 3 square kilometres in the east, and a single bus depot. In 2021 Navpur covered 95 square kilometres and had a population of 18 lakh. The northern farmland had been replaced by housing colonies and an IT park, a second bridge had been built, a metro line ran from the old centre to the IT park, and the lake had shrunk to 1.5 square kilometres because of construction along its banks. Write an analytical paragraph of 100-120 words describing the changes and drawing a conclusion.
valuePoints: Introduction: what the maps show (Navpur in 2001 and 2021)
Growth: area more than doubled from 40 to 95 sq km, and population rose 140% from 7.5 lakh to 18 lakh
Land use: northern farmland replaced by housing colonies and an IT park
Infrastructure: a second bridge and a metro line from the old centre to the IT park
Environmental cost: the lake halved from 3 to 1.5 sq km because of construction on its banks
Supported conclusion: rapid development improved jobs and transport but at the cost of farmland and the lake, so future growth needs planning that protects them

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Changes in size, population, land use, transport and the lake described accurately, with a balanced conclusion

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Changes grouped sensibly rather than listed feature by feature, with an introduction and conclusion

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Correct grammar, especially past and past perfect forms for change over time

questions.stem: A flow chart describes how a school recycling drive turned plastic bottles into T-shirts in one term. Step 1: 10,000 plastic bottles were collected. Step 2: they were sorted; 8,500 clean PET bottles were kept and 1,500 contaminated bottles were rejected. Step 3: the 8,500 bottles, at 20 grams each, were washed and shredded into 170 kg of flakes. Step 4: the flakes were melted into pellets; 20 kg were lost in washing and melting, leaving 150 kg of pellets. Step 5: the pellets were spun into polyester fibre and made into 300 T-shirts, using 0.5 kg each. Write an analytical paragraph of 100-120 words describing the process and drawing a conclusion.
valuePoints: Introduction: what the flow chart shows (the five stages from bottle collection to T-shirts)
The stages described in order with sequencing words: collection, sorting, washing and shredding, melting into pellets, spinning into fibre and making T-shirts
Losses: 15% of bottles (1,500 of 10,000) rejected at sorting; 20 kg of 170 kg flakes lost in processing
Output: 150 kg of pellets made 300 T-shirts, so roughly 28 bottles went into each T-shirt (8,500 / 300)
Supported conclusion: recycling turns waste into a useful product, and cleaner collection would reduce the largest loss

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Every stage with its figures, the losses identified and a conclusion the data supports

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Stages in the correct sequence with clear sequencing connectors

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Correct grammar, especially the passive voice for describing a process

questions.stem: A table shows how 120 Class 10 students of a school spent their study time per week in the month before the board examinations, in two groups: the 48 students who scored above 80% in the pre-board examination, and the other 72 students. Average hours per week, above-80% group and other group: self-study from the textbook 10 and 8; solving sample papers 8 and 3; coaching classes 4 and 6; online video lessons 2 and 4; group study 1 and 2. Totals: 25 hours and 23 hours. Write an analytical paragraph of 100-120 words comparing the two groups and drawing a conclusion.
valuePoints: Introduction: what the table shows (weekly study time by method for 48 higher-scoring and 72 other students)
Total study time is similar: 25 hours against 23, a difference of only 2 hours
The biggest difference is in solving sample papers: 8 hours against 3
Higher scorers also spend more time on textbook self-study (10 against 8) but less on coaching (4 against 6), videos (2 against 4) and group study (1 against 2)
Supported conclusion: how students study seems to matter more than how long, with active practice linked to higher scores; the data shows a link, not proof of cause

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Totals and each method compared with correct figures, the largest difference identified, and a carefully supported conclusion

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Comparison organised by similarity and difference, with an introduction and conclusion

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Correct grammar and precise comparative language (whereas, while, compared with)
